title: Shares, exchanges and tickers

inOneLine.simple: A share is a small piece of ownership in a company. Shares are bought and sold on an exchange, under a short code called a ticker.
inOneLine.balanced: A [[share]] is a fractional claim on a company's profits and assets. Your stake = your shares ÷ shares outstanding. Shares trade on a [[stock-exchange]] under a [[ticker]], and the price is set by buyers and sellers, not by the company.

explain.simple: Imagine a company split into 50 million equal pieces. Each piece is one share. If you own some of those pieces, you own a small part of the business. Shares are traded on a stock exchange, a market with rules about who can list and how orders are matched. Each company has a short code of letters, its ticker, so it fits on a quote screen. The price you see is simply the last price a buyer and a seller agreed on.
explain.balanced: Owning shares gives you a share of future profits if the company pays them out as [[dividend|dividends]], and usually a vote. It does not give you a fixed return: the price can fall as well as rise, and the company owes shareholders nothing back. If the company issues new shares, each existing share becomes a smaller slice. Tickers can look alike, so always check the full company name before you place even a simulated order.

assumptions: Fictional company with 50 million shares outstanding
You buy 500 shares at 8.00 USD each; costs ignored
Illustrative dividend of 0.20 USD per share; a learning example, not a forecast
steps: Your stake = 500 ÷ 50,000,000 = 0.00001, which is 0.001% of the company.
A dividend of 0.20 USD per share pays you 500 × 0.20 = 100 USD.
If the price falls to 6.00 USD, your shares are worth 500 × 6.00 = 3,000 USD: 1,000 USD less than you paid, a 25% fall.

assumptions: Same fictional company and your same 500 shares
The company issues 10 million new shares, so there are now 60 million
steps: You own the same number of shares, but a smaller slice of the company.
Each share now has a claim on a smaller part of the profit, unless the new money helps profit grow enough to make up for it.

explainSimpler: A share is a slice of a company. The exchange is where slices are swapped. The ticker is the slice's name tag.
commonMistake: Thinking that a share price of 1 USD is "cheap" and 100 USD is "expensive". The price of one share means little without knowing how many shares there are and how much the company earns.

quickCheck.prompt: A fictional company has 20 million shares. You own 2,000. What fraction of the company do you own?
Who sets the price of a share on an exchange?

options.text: The company, at its yearly meeting
options.explanation: No: the company does not set its trading price.

options.text: The exchange, using a fixed formula
options.explanation: No: the exchange matches orders, it does not choose the price.
Right: the price is where buyers and sellers last agreed.

quickCheck.prompt: Two companies have tickers that differ by one letter. What should you do before a simulated order?

options.explanation: Right: similar tickers can belong to very different companies.

options.text: Pick the one with the lower price
options.explanation: No: a lower price per share says nothing about value.

options.text: Assume they are the same firm
options.explanation: No: similar codes can be unrelated companies.

doItNow.instructions: Open Practice → Paper trading and choose the "Practice ordinary share" instrument. Note the simulated bid and ask. Place a simulated buy of 10 shares and write down what it cost, then what you would get if you sold straight away at the bid.

homework: In one sentence each, explain to a friend what a share, an exchange and a ticker are.
